rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, 3-year field experiment at Citra FL with own yield, soil water and root core data. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 5, root length density sampled at three positions across the bed under drip; independent of date RLD fell 41% from the drip line (P1) to P2 and 70% to P3, roots concentrated around the emitters; Table 4 shows position x depth effects. Q9: Section 3.3 reports RLD at P1 0-15 cm at 66 DAT as 10.5 +/- 3.9 cm cm-3 for SDI vs 2.6 +/- 1.7 and 2.5 +/- 0.9 for SUR and TIME.
rows.notes: All treatments are drip (surface or subsurface) so there is no non-drip comparator; the study shows roots concentrate near drip/fertigation lines on this sandy soil but does not measure lateral soil water movement (TDR probes were placed 5 cm from the drip line, not across the bed) nor does it show a yield harm from this distribution - in fact SMS-based drip increased yield. Root sampling was in one season (2006) at one N rate only. Dispersion values are given only for one position/depth; other RLD tables carry letter groupings only. Q4 no because the limiting lateral wetting mechanism is asserted, not measured. Q8 no: no explicit limitation stated for the root result.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own 3-year field experiment. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 2, SMS-controlled drip (SUR, SDI) with up to five short daily irrigation windows increased marketable yield 69-80% (2005), 20-26% (2006) and 11-21% (2007) over fixed-time irrigation, and above-ground biomass was higher. Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, TDR soil moisture showed SMS treatments kept soil water relatively constant with almost no spikes at 25-55 cm, while TIME showed percolation spikes; Section 3.3 reports residual soil nitrate in 0-30 cm of 32 and 12 mg kg-1 for SDI and SUR vs 2 for TIME, linked to higher biomass and yield. Q8: Section 2, authors state TIME used twin lines for experimental convenience whereas a grower would use a single line; Section 3.1, probe position relative to the buried drip line in SDI caused higher water application.
rows.notes: Yield measured by harvest grading only (one method). Single site, soil and crop. No condition stated as a requirement for the yield effect; the statement that the effect applies to low water-holding-capacity soils is a scope remark. Table 2 reports means with Duncan letters only; Table 1 gives ANOVA CV% but no SD/SE/CI for treatment means, so Q9 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, SMS-based treatments irrigated briefly with small soil moisture increases and almost no percolation spikes at 25-55 cm, whereas TIME showed pronounced spikes indicating percolation; Section 3.3, soil nitrate at 74 DAT in 0-30 cm was 32 (SDI) and 12 (SUR) vs 2 mg kg-1 (TIME), interpreted as reduced N displacement/leaching under frequent small applications. Q3: two independent methods - TDR soil water monitoring at two depths (Section 2.3, Fig. 4) and KCl-extracted soil nitrate sampling by depth (Sections 2.3, 3.3). Q4: soil water content and percolation spikes measured by TDR as the intermediate variable for leaching. Q8: Section 3.1, authors note TDR position (0-25 cm) relative to the 15 cm deep drip line meant SDI soil moisture variations were not captured as distinctly; Section 2, TIME twin-line arrangement differs from grower practice.
rows.notes: Leaching is inferred from soil moisture spikes and residual soil nitrate rather than measured directly (no lysimeters or drainage collection). Soil nitrate comparison reported for one sampling date. The reference to sandy soil's low water holding capacity explains percolation under TIME but is not stated as a requirement. No dispersion given for the soil nitrate or soil water results (initial nitrate +/- values only), so Q9 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own 3-year field trial. Q2: Abstract, Section 3.1, Fig. 2 and Conclusions, SMS-controlled surface drip used 15-51% less irrigation water than fixed-time irrigation (40-51% in 2006-2007) and SMS-controlled SDI 7-29% less; iWUE ranked SUR > SDI > TIME (Table 2). Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, the controller bypassed events when VWC exceeded the 0.10 m3 m-3 threshold and TDR data show stable soil moisture without percolation spikes, versus spikes and rapid drainage under TIME. Q8: Section 3.1, authors attribute the smaller SDI savings to probe placement relative to the buried drip line; Section 2, TIME twin-line setup was for experimental convenience and differs from grower practice.
rows.notes: The review's figures (40-65% savings, 11-45% yield gain) do not match the study's reported 15-51% / 7-29% savings and 11-80% yield gains. Irrigation volume measured by flowmeters only (one method). Single site/soil/crop. Probe placement is offered as a hedged explanation, not stated as a requirement, so Q7 no. Savings given as year ranges; iWUE means with letters and ANOVA CV% only, no SD/SE/CI, so Q9 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 2, marketable yield for SMS-controlled treatments was 69-80%, 20-26% and 11-21% higher than TIME in 2005, 2006 and 2007; abstract reports 11-80% higher yield. Q4: Section 3.1/Fig. 4 TDR soil moisture dynamics and Section 3.3 residual soil nitrate (32 and 12 vs 2 mg kg-1 in 0-30 cm) measured as the pathway from scheduling to yield. Q8: Section 2, TIME twin-line arrangement for convenience unlike grower practice; Section 3.1, probe position relative to drip line affected SDI water application.
rows.notes: Review's 11-45% yield range does not match the study's 11-80%. Yield from harvest grading only. One site, soil and crop. No stated requirement for the effect. Means with letter groupings and ANOVA CV% only; Q9 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own small-plot 3-year field trial. Q2: Section 2 describes ECH2O capacitance probes triggering irrigation at a 0.10 m3 m-3 threshold; Section 3.1, Fig. 2 and Conclusions report 15-51% (SUR) and 7-29% (SDI) less irrigation than fixed-time scheduling in drip-irrigated fresh-market tomato. Q4: Section 3.1 and Fig. 4, bypassed events and TDR-measured soil moisture show reduced percolation as the mechanism of water savings. Q8: Section 3.1, SDI savings limited by probe placement relative to the buried drip line; Section 2, TIME twin-line arrangement differs from commercial practice.
rows.notes: Flowmeter measurement only (one method). Single site, sandy soil, one crop. No requirement stated; probe placement given as explanation. No SD/SE/CI for water application or iWUE means (letters and CV% only).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 2, capacitance-sensor-controlled drip treatments gave 11-80% higher marketable tomato yield than fixed-time irrigation across 2005-2007, with higher biomass. Q4: Section 3.1/Fig. 4 soil moisture dynamics and Section 3.3 residual soil nitrate measured as intermediate variables explaining the yield response. Q8: Section 2, TIME control used twin lines for experimental convenience unlike grower practice; Section 3.1, probe placement issue for SDI.
rows.notes: Yield by harvest grading only. One site/soil/crop. No stated requirement for the yield effect. Table 2 means with Duncan letters and Table 1 CV% only; no SD/SE/CI, so Q9 no.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a 3-year single-site plastic-mulch drip tomato trial on Florida sand comparing SMS-controlled surface and subsurface drip against fixed-time irrigation at three N rates; all treatments use drip, so for the drip row there is no non-drip comparator. Reported water savings (15-51% SUR, 7-29% SDI) and yield gains (11-80%) differ from the figures quoted in the review passages.
